articles.title: Oil prices fall and shares jump after US-Iran deal announced
articles.summaryB1: The United States and Iran have reached a deal that could bring major changes to global oil markets. As part of the agreement, the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Middle East, will be reopened. This strait is one of the most essential shipping routes in the world. About 20% of the world's oil passes through it, so when it is blocked or threatened, oil prices usually rise sharply. Following the announcement by US President Donald Trump, oil prices dropped and stock markets around the world saw shares jump in value. This happened because investors felt more confident about the future supply of oil. The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, and Iran has the power to disrupt traffic through it. Tensions between the US and Iran have been high for many years, mostly because of disagreements over Iran's nuclear programme and economic sanctions placed on Iran by the US. A deal between these two countries is therefore seen as a step toward greater stability in the region. Many people hope this agreement will lower energy costs and help the global economy recover. However, some experts warn that it is too early to celebrate, as similar deals in the past have sometimes failed to last.

Central to the agreement is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow but strategically vital passage through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply flows daily. President Donald Trump confirmed the accord, signalling a potential thaw in one of the most fraught diplomatic relationships of recent decades. The US and Iran have long been at odds over Tehran's nuclear ambitions, with successive rounds of economic sanctions severely curtailing Iran's ability to export oil and participate in international trade. The prospect of eased tensions has led investors to reckon with a future of more predictable energy supply, driving the market rally observed following the announcement. However, analysts caution that optimism should be tempered. Previous diplomatic overtures between Washington and Tehran have often stalled or collapsed under political pressure from hardliners on both sides. The geopolitical implications of such an accord extend well beyond oil prices. A sustained agreement could reshape alliances in the Middle East, affect the calculations of other regional powers, and influence ongoing negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme. articles.title: The US and Iran have agreed a deal. How soon could things go back to normal?
articles.summaryB1: The United States and Iran have agreed a deal, and many people are asking how quickly life can return to normal. For years, the two countries have had a very difficult relationship. The US placed strict sanctions on Iran, which means it stopped other countries from doing business with Iran. This hurt Iran's economy badly. Now, with a new agreement in place, there is hope that trade and oil exports from Iran could start again. Oil is one of Iran's most valuable products, and when Iran cannot sell it freely, global oil prices can go up. This affects people all over the world, including the cost of fuel and everyday goods. However, experts warn that the impact of the conflict will continue to affect the global economy for several months. Rebuilding trust between countries takes time, and businesses need to feel confident before they start investing again. Banks and companies will also need to check new rules carefully before they act. So while the deal is a positive step, a full recovery will not happen overnight. People in many countries are watching closely, hoping that stability will bring lower prices and more economic growth in the near future.

articles.title: David Hockney depicted a 'peaceful, gay paradise' when homosexuality was a crime
articles.summaryB1: David Hockney is one of Britain's most famous painters. He is known for breaking social taboos – things that society considers wrong or forbidden to talk about or show. In the 1960s, homosexuality was illegal in Britain. This means that gay men could be arrested and sent to prison just for being who they were. Despite this danger, Hockney painted pictures that celebrated same-sex relationships openly and joyfully. His art showed gay men living normal, happy lives together. Many people described his work as creating a 'peaceful, gay paradise' – an ideal world where love between men was free and accepted. Hockney moved to California in the 1960s, where the atmosphere felt more relaxed and tolerant. This change gave him more freedom to express himself through his art. His paintings challenged the attitudes of the time and helped people see gay relationships in a positive, human way. Today, Hockney is recognised not only as a brilliant artist but also as someone who was brave enough to depict real life honestly, even when it was dangerous to do so. His work reminds us how much society has changed – and why art can be a powerful way to challenge unfair rules.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it was brave for Hockney to depict same-sex relationships in his art when homosexuality was illegal?
articles.summaryB2: David Hockney, one of the defining figures of twentieth-century British art, deliberately broke social taboos by portraying same-sex relationships with warmth and openness at a time when homosexuality was a criminal offence in the United Kingdom. Criminalised until 1967, gay men in Britain faced arrest, prosecution, and public humiliation simply for existing authentically. Against this backdrop of repression, Hockney's canvases offered something radical: a vision of gay life as tender, ordinary, and worthy of artistic celebration. Critics and commentators have described his work as conjuring a 'peaceful, gay paradise' – an unapologetic affirmation of love and identity that stood in direct defiance of prevailing social norms. Hockney relocated to California in the 1960s, drawn by a cultural climate that felt considerably more permissive than Britain's. There, his iconic swimming pool paintings and intimate double portraits became testaments to a freer mode of living. What makes Hockney's achievement particularly striking is not merely the aesthetic quality of his work, but its quiet subversiveness. By refusing to conceal or sanitise gay experience, he compelled viewers to confront their own assumptions and prejudices. His art functioned as a form of quiet advocacy long before the language of LGBTQ+ rights entered mainstream discourse. Today, Hockney's legacy endures as a reminder that art can humanise those whom society marginalises, and that visibility itself can be an act of resistance.

articles.title: Six ways to keep your home and yourself cool in hot weather
articles.summaryB1: When the weather gets very hot, it can be hard to stay comfortable at home. Luckily, there are six simple things you can do to keep your house cool without spending a lot of money. First, you should block sunlight by closing curtains or blinds during the day, especially on windows that face the sun. This stops heat from building up inside. Second, you can ventilate your home by opening windows early in the morning and late at night, when the outside air is cooler. During the hottest part of the day, keep windows closed. Third, using electric fans wisely helps a lot. Placing a bowl of ice in front of a fan can make the air feel colder. Fourth, you should avoid using ovens or other appliances that generate a lot of heat. Cook outside or eat cold meals instead. Fifth, keeping yourself hydrated by drinking plenty of water is very helpful. Your body stays cooler when you drink regularly. Sixth, you can cool your body directly by taking cold showers or putting cold, damp cloths on your wrists and neck. These methods are easy to try at home. As summers become hotter in many countries, knowing how to stay cool is becoming more and more useful for everyone.

A BBC Science & Environment article outlines six evidence-based strategies for keeping both your home and your body cool during hot weather, without relying on energy-intensive air conditioning. The first strategy involves thermal regulation through shading — closing curtains and blinds on sun-facing windows during peak hours to prevent solar heat from accumulating indoors. The second recommendation is strategic ventilation: opening windows in the cooler hours of early morning and late evening, then sealing the house during the hottest part of the day to trap cooler air inside. Third, fans can be used more effectively by placing ice in front of them, a low-tech method that mimics the cooling effect of an air conditioner. Fourth, residents are advised to minimise the use of heat-generating appliances such as ovens, opting instead for cold meals or outdoor cooking. Fifth, maintaining personal hydration is highlighted as essential, since the body regulates its own temperature partly through fluid intake. Finally, direct body cooling — through cold showers or damp cloths applied to pulse points like the wrists — offers immediate relief. Together, these measures reflect a pragmatic approach to climate adaptation at the household level, one that prioritises accessibility and affordability over technological solutions.

articles.title: Norwegian crown princess's son found guilty of two counts of rape
articles.summaryB1: Marius Borg Høiby, who is 29 years old, is the son of Norway's Crown Princess Mette-Marit. A court in Norway has found him guilty of two counts of rape. Crown Princess Mette-Marit is married to Crown Prince Haakon, who will one day become the King of Norway. Marius Borg Høiby is not a member of the royal family himself, but he grew up in the royal household and has often appeared in public with his mother. A court must decide if a person is guilty or not guilty of a crime. In this case, the judge decided there was enough evidence to convict him on both charges. The verdict means he will spend four years behind bars. Cases like this are difficult for royal families because they happen in the public eye. Many people follow news about royal families closely, so this case received a lot of media attention. The Norwegian royal family has not made any official public statement about the verdict so far. This case reminds us that justice systems apply to everyone, regardless of their family background or social status.

articles.title: Global stocks power to record highs as deal ignites ‘risk on’ rally
articles.summaryB1:
Global stock markets reached record high levels recently, driven by positive news about trade and business. Investors became more confident after a major trade deal was announced, which helped push share prices up around the world. When investors feel confident, they are more willing to take risks and buy stocks, which is known as a 'risk on' mood in financial markets.

One piece of good news came from the United States and another country reaching an agreement to reduce trade barriers. This kind of deal can help companies sell more products abroad, which usually leads to higher profits and rising stock prices.

Another boost came from SpaceX, the private space company owned by Elon Musk. SpaceX completed a historic initial public offering, meaning that for the first time, ordinary people could buy shares in the company. This was seen as a major milestone for the private space industry and generated a lot of excitement among investors.

An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company sells its shares to the public for the first time. It allows companies to raise large amounts of money to fund future growth.

Together, these two events improved investor sentiment worldwide. When markets rise like this, it can signal that people feel optimistic about the economy. However, experts often remind us that stock markets can change direction quickly, so caution is always advisable.

However, analysts frequently caution that sentiment-driven gains can be fragile if the underlying economic fundamentals do not support them.

The listing of Elon Musk's private space company was described as historic, marking a rare moment when a high-profile, previously closely held enterprise opened itself to public markets. From a Polish investor's perspective, movements in global equities matter because many pension funds and investment portfolios have exposure to international markets. A sustained rally can increase the value of savings, though it also raises questions about whether current valuations are justified by real economic performance.

articles.title: EU orders Meta to open WhatsApp to rival AI chatbots
articles.summaryB1: The European Union has told Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, that it must open its messaging app to AI chatbots made by other companies. This means that rival companies, like OpenAI, could connect their AI assistants to WhatsApp. The EU says this is necessary to make sure there is fair competition in the technology market. Meta strongly disagrees with this decision. The company has accused the EU of going too far with its rules, calling it 'regulatory overreach'. Meta also warns that the decision could actually help large tech giants like OpenAI, giving them free access to WhatsApp's huge user base. This seems to go against what the EU wants, which is to reduce the power of big tech companies. The EU has been working hard to control how the biggest technology platforms operate in Europe. The rules that apply here are part of the Digital Markets Act, a law designed to give smaller companies a fair chance to compete. Many people support stronger regulation of big tech, but others worry that some rules can have unexpected results. This case shows how difficult it can be for governments to regulate technology companies effectively. It is not yet clear exactly how or when Meta will be required to make these changes.

articles.title: El Niño forms in Pacific as experts say it will likely turbocharge extreme weather
articles.summaryB1:
El Niño has officially arrived in the Pacific Ocean. Scientists in the United States confirmed this on Thursday. El Niño is a natural weather event that happens when the water near the equator in the Pacific Ocean becomes warmer than usual. This warm water affects weather patterns all over the world. It can cause more rain in some places and droughts in others.

US forecasters from an organisation called NOAA made the announcement. They predict that this El Niño could become the strongest of the entire century by autumn. That means it may be more powerful than any El Niño we have ever recorded.

The head of the United Nations also spoke about this event. He called it an urgent climate warning. This means he believes it is a sign that our planet is in serious danger from climate change.

El Niño works by changing global weather patterns. When it is strong, extreme weather events such as heavy storms, floods, and heatwaves become more likely. Experts worry that because climate change is already making weather more extreme, this El Niño could make things even worse.

For people around the world, this news means that unusual and dangerous weather may be coming. Governments and organisations are watching the situation carefully to prepare for possible disasters.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think strong extreme weather events are becoming more dangerous for people around the world today?
articles.summaryB2:
El Niño, the powerful climate phenomenon characterised by abnormally warm surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific, has officially formed, US authorities confirmed on Thursday. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) made the announcement, warning that the event could intensify to historic levels by autumn, potentially making it the most severe El Niño of the 21st century.

The phenomenon disrupts established atmospheric circulation systems, triggering cascading effects on global weather — bringing prolonged rainfall and flooding to some regions while exposing others to intense drought and wildfires. Scientists are particularly alarmed because the arrival of El Niño coincides with already elevated global temperatures driven by human-induced climate change, a combination that could amplify the destructive potential of extreme weather events worldwide.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres responded to the news by describing the development as an urgent climate warning, framing it not merely as a meteorological occurrence but as further evidence of a worsening planetary emergency. His statement reflects a growing consensus among climate scientists that natural climate variability and anthropogenic warming are increasingly overlapping in ways that compound their individual impacts.

articles.title: Trump settles for a truce of convenience

President Trump had promised that Iran would have to give up completely — what he called 'unconditional surrender' — but the final deal looks very different. Iran did not collapse under pressure. Instead, it came out of the negotiations in a stronger position than many people expected. The agreement is being described as a 'truce of convenience', which means both sides stopped fighting for practical reasons, not because one side truly won. Iran still has its nuclear programme and has not given up its main sources of power. Trump wanted a big victory, but critics say the result is more of a compromise. For Iran, surviving the conflict without making major concessions is itself a kind of success. The situation matters because Iran's position in the Middle East affects oil prices, regional security, and the foreign policy of many countries. The United States spent a lot of political energy on this confrontation. Now, both governments must decide what comes next. Scientists are concerned because the planet is already warming due to human activity. Adding El Niño on top of this could push temperatures to dangerous new levels. Regions already vulnerable to climate instability face a particularly acute risk: parts of South America may experience severe flooding, while Australia, southern Africa, and Southeast Asia could face prolonged dry spells and crop failures. Meteorologists are urging governments to treat El Niño as a catalyst for reviewing disaster preparedness strategies, given that the combination of natural variability and anthropogenic climate change creates compounding risks. articles.title: Anthropic to disable its most advanced AI models after US order limiting foreign access

The episode highlights a deepening tension between the commercial ambitions of AI companies and the tightening regulatory grip of governments seeking to treat advanced AI as a matter of national security. articles.title: What is in the US-Iran deal?
articles.summaryB1: The United States and Iran have made a new agreement that could reduce tension between the two countries. The deal will extend a ceasefire for 60 more days. A ceasefire means both sides agree to stop fighting or threatening each other. The agreement will also reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of water between Iran and Oman. This strait is one of the most important shipping routes in the world. About 20% of the world's oil passes through it, so keeping it open matters a great deal to global trade. If Iran blocked this waterway, oil prices around the world could rise sharply. The third part of the deal involves nuclear talks. Iran and the US will begin negotiations about Iran's nuclear programme. Many countries worry that Iran wants to build nuclear weapons, which Iran denies. These talks are a chance to find a peaceful solution. This agreement is good news for businesses and governments that depend on stable oil supplies. However, it is only a temporary solution. The ceasefire lasts just 60 days, so both sides must work quickly to reach a longer and more permanent deal. The outcome of the nuclear negotiations will be watched closely by countries around the world.

articles.summaryB2: A tentative but consequential agreement between the United States and Iran has emerged, comprising three interlocking elements: a 60-day extension of an existing ceasefire, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the commencement of formal nuclear negotiations. The Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint of immense strategic and economic weight — roughly a fifth of global oil supplies transit through this narrow waterway, making any disruption to its passage a potential catalyst for energy market instability worldwide. Iran's capacity to threaten closure of the strait has long been regarded as one of its most potent tools of geopolitical pressure. The resumption of nuclear talks is perhaps the most contentious aspect of the agreement. Western powers have repeatedly accused Tehran of pursuing weapons-grade enrichment, allegations Iran consistently refutes. Previous diplomatic frameworks, most notably the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, collapsed after the US withdrew in 2018 under the Trump administration, leaving a deep deficit of trust on both sides. The 60-day timeframe underlines just how provisional this arrangement remains. articles.title: Oil prices slide after US-Iran deal announced
articles.summaryB1:
Oil prices around the world dropped sharply after the United States and Iran announced a new agreement. Under this deal, the Strait of Hormuz, a vital sea route in the Middle East, will be reopened. US President Donald Trump made the announcement, and the news quickly affected global oil markets.

When the strait was blocked or threatened, oil prices went up because traders worried about supply. Now that the two countries have reached an agreement, traders expect more oil to flow freely again, so prices have fallen.

The relationship between the US and Iran has been difficult for many years. Iran is a major oil producer, and tensions between the two countries often affect energy markets worldwide. This new deal could mean that Iranian oil returns to international markets in larger quantities.

For everyday people, lower oil prices can mean cheaper fuel for cars and lower heating costs. However, some experts warn that such agreements can be fragile and may not last. It is still too early to know if this deal will hold. The situation is being watched carefully by governments, businesses, and consumers around the world.

articles.title: ‘Super El Niño’ is officially here, scientists say. What can we expect?
articles.summaryB1: El Niño has officially arrived, according to scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) in the United States. This is a natural weather pattern that happens in the Pacific Ocean, but this time it could be unusually powerful. Experts are calling it a 'super El Niño' and say it may be the strongest of the century so far. Forecasters had already predicted that this phenomenon would develop during the summer months. When El Niño occurs, it warms ocean waters in the Pacific, and this affects weather all around the world. A super El Niño can supercharge extreme weather events, making storms, floods, and droughts worse than normal. Scientists are also warning that global temperatures could reach record highs because of it. This is especially worrying because temperatures are already rising due to climate change. When El Niño combines with the general warming of the planet, the effects can be very serious. People living in areas that are already affected by extreme weather may face even greater challenges. Understanding this phenomenon helps governments and communities prepare for what could be a very difficult period of unusual and dangerous weather conditions around the world.

The confirmation comes after months of anticipation, with forecasters having already flagged the likelihood of such an event emerging over the summer. A super El Niño is expected to supercharge these effects, potentially pushing global temperatures to unprecedented record highs. Scientists warn that when El Niño overlaps with the existing warming trend, the compounding effect on global temperatures can be dramatic and far-reaching. articles.title: UK sets out AI infrastructure push at London Tech Week – how does it stack up?
articles.summaryB1: During London Tech Week, the UK government announced plans to spend billions of pounds on artificial intelligence. The goal is to build better AI infrastructure, which means the systems and tools needed to develop and run AI technology. This includes chips, which are small electronic parts that power computers and AI programmes. The government wants the UK to have more control over these technologies, which are currently dominated by the United States and China. Officials also talked about skills training and new rules for social media. Some of the announcements were completely new ideas, while others were updates to plans already shared before. Countries around the world are trying to assert their position in the AI economy, meaning they want a strong role in how this technology develops. For the UK government, London Tech Week was a chance to show that the country has a clear growth story. However, journalists and experts are asking questions about whether these proposals will actually work in practice. articles.title: Rare footage captured of Great White shark in Mediterranean Sea
articles.summaryB1:

The encounter happened in the waters between Tunisia, a country in North Africa, and Sicily, an island in southern Italy. The diver said he was shaking while he recorded the rare footage of the shark underwater.

Great White sharks are endangered animals, which means there are very few of them left in the world. Seeing one in the Mediterranean Sea is very unusual. Scientists and wildlife experts say that Great White sharks rarely appear in this part of the world, so this video is very important.

The footage that the diver captured is now helping people learn more about these animals and where they live. Great White sharks are often seen as dangerous, but they are also a protected species because their numbers have fallen so much over the years.

Many people are excited about the video because it shows that Great White sharks still exist in the Mediterranean. Conservation groups hope that rare sightings like this one will help the public understand why it is important to protect these animals. The diver was brave to keep filming even though he was afraid. articles.title: 'No dead ends': What the Dutch can teach us about tackling youth unemployment
articles.summaryB1:
Youth unemployment is a big problem in many countries. Young people who are not studying, working, or doing any training are sometimes called 'NEET' – Not in Education, Employment, or Training. Having too many young people in this situation can cause serious problems for society and the economy.

The Netherlands has found very effective ways to tackle this problem. The country has one of the lowest rates of young NEETs in the world, among people aged 16 to 24. This is a great achievement, and other countries want to understand how the Dutch system works.

One important idea in the Netherlands is that young people should never reach a dead end – a situation where they have no options and nowhere to go. The Dutch system tries to make sure there is always a next step available for every young person, whether that is more education, a job, or professional training.

Government support plays a key role in this. Local authorities work closely with young people to find out what they need and help them move forward. Early action is also very important – problems are identified quickly before they become worse.

Other countries could learn a lot from the Dutch approach. When young people have opportunities and support, they can build better futures. This benefits not only the individuals but also the whole of society.

articles.summaryB2:
Youth unemployment remains one of the most persistent socioeconomic challenges facing developed nations, yet the Netherlands has emerged as a striking exception. The country consistently records one of the world's lowest proportions of 16 to 24-year-olds classified as NEET – Not in Education, Employment, or Training – a benchmark increasingly used by policymakers to gauge how effectively societies are integrating young people into productive life.

Central to the Dutch model is a philosophy of ensuring there are, in the words used to describe the approach, 'no dead ends'. Rather than allowing young people to fall through the cracks of bureaucratic systems, the Netherlands has built a framework designed to keep every pathway open. Whether through vocational training, apprenticeships, or targeted employment schemes, the emphasis is on early intervention and personalised support before disengagement becomes entrenched.

Local municipalities play a pivotal role, working proactively to identify at-risk individuals and connect them with appropriate resources. This decentralised approach allows for tailored responses rather than one-size-fits-all policy, arguably one of its greatest strengths.

The implications for other nations are considerable. High NEET rates carry long-term costs – not only for the individuals concerned, whose prospects narrow significantly over time, but for wider society through lost productivity and increased welfare dependency. The Dutch example suggests that sustained investment in youth support systems, combined with structural flexibility, can yield measurable and lasting results.

This is worrying for many countries because extreme weather can damage homes, destroy crops, and affect millions of people. Governments and scientists are monitoring the situation closely so they can warn communities in advance. It is important for people to understand that natural events like El Niño and human-caused climate change can work together to boost temperatures to dangerous levels. articles.title: I wanted to quit Eurovision twice - then won it, says Bangaranga singer Dara

articles.title: The gamers taking on the industry to stop it switching off games
articles.summaryB1:

The campaign is called Stop Killing Games. It is asking governments to create new rules that would force publishers to keep games playable after they close the official servers. For example, they want companies to release special software so players can run the game themselves.

This is becoming a bigger problem because many modern games need an internet connection to work. If the company decides to shut down the servers, the game simply stops working forever. Players feel this is unfair because they own the game but cannot use it.

The campaign has already collected hundreds of thousands of signatures across Europe. Supporters argue that when you buy something, you should be able to keep using it. Publishers, however, say that running servers costs money and they cannot do it forever.

This debate raises an important question about digital ownership. Do you really own a game if a company can switch it off? Many players believe that consumers deserve better protection. The outcome of this campaign could change how the gaming industry works in the future.

articles.summaryB2:
A grassroots movement known as Stop Killing Games is mounting a significant challenge to the established practices of the video game industry, specifically targeting the widespread phenomenon of publishers permanently deactivating titles without ensuring any form of continued playability for consumers.

articles.title: Armenia's pro-West government wins election despite Russian pressure

articles.title: Spain's visitor numbers hit new highs as tourists avoid Middle East
articles.summaryB1:
Spain has broken a record for tourism. In April 2024, the country welcomed 9.1 million international visitors. This is the highest number ever recorded for the month of April. It is a very positive sign for Spain's tourist industry.

One important reason for this increase is the situation in the Middle East. Because of conflict in that region, many tourists have decided to avoid travelling there. Instead, they are choosing safer destinations in Europe, and Spain is one of the most popular choices.

Spain is already one of the most visited countries in the world. It attracts tourists because of its warm weather, beautiful beaches, historic cities, and delicious food. Places like Barcelona, Madrid, and the Canary Islands are especially popular.

The record numbers are good news for the Spanish economy. Tourism creates many jobs and brings a lot of money into the country. Hotels, restaurants, and transport companies all benefit when more visitors arrive.

However, some people are concerned about the impact of so many tourists. In some cities, local residents have complained that tourism makes housing more expensive and public spaces more crowded. Balancing the benefits and problems of tourism is a challenge that Spain will need to manage carefully in the future.

articles.summaryB2:
Spain has set a new benchmark in international tourism, recording 9.1 million foreign visitors in April 2024 — the highest figure ever for that month. A significant driver behind the surge appears to be ongoing instability in the Middle East. With conflict deterring travellers from visiting popular destinations in that region, many tourists have redirected their plans towards Mediterranean Europe, with Spain emerging as a clear beneficiary. This trend reflects a broader pattern of demand displacement, whereby geopolitical tensions in one region channel tourist flows towards perceived safer alternatives.

For the Spanish economy, the implications are largely positive. Tourism is a cornerstone of the country's GDP, supporting hundreds of thousands of jobs across hospitality, transport, and retail sectors. Record visitor numbers translate directly into increased revenue for businesses and greater tax receipts for the government.

Nevertheless, the boom is not without controversy. Anti-tourism sentiment has been growing in several Spanish cities, where residents argue that mass tourism inflates housing costs, strains public infrastructure, and erodes local culture. articles.title: Exploding rocket casts doubts over Nasa's Moon plans
articles.summaryB1:
A large rocket built by a company called Blue Origin exploded during a test. This is bad news for both Blue Origin and for Nasa, the American space agency. Nasa had chosen Blue Origin to help build a special spacecraft that would land astronauts on the Moon. This is part of Nasa's Artemis programme, which plans to send humans back to the Moon for the first time in more than fifty years.

The rocket that exploded is called New Glenn. It was being tested when something went wrong and it was destroyed. Nobody was hurt because there were no people on board. However, the accident is a serious setback for the programme. A setback means something that slows down your progress or makes your plans more difficult.

Blue Origin is owned by Jeff Bezos, who also started the online shopping company Amazon. The company has been working hard to compete with other private space companies, such as SpaceX.

Nasa is already facing delays with its Moon mission. This explosion makes the situation more difficult. Scientists and engineers will need to investigate what went wrong before the rocket can be used again. Many people are now asking whether Nasa will be able to send astronauts to the Moon on schedule. The coming months will be very important for the future of this ambitious space programme.

articles.summaryB2:
An explosion involving a Blue Origin rocket has cast serious doubts over Nasa's already troubled plans to return astronauts to the Moon. The rocket destroyed in the explosion is New Glenn, Blue Origin's flagship launch vehicle. While no crew members were on board and there were no reported casualties, the loss of the vehicle is a considerable technical and financial setback. Engineers will now need to conduct a thorough investigation to determine the root cause of the failure before flight operations can resume.

The explosion compounds the difficulties already facing Nasa's Moon programme, which has endured repeated delays and rising costs. Critics have long questioned whether the agency's timeline is realistic, and this latest mishap is likely to intensify that scrutiny. Blue Origin has been striving to establish itself as a credible competitor in an increasingly crowded commercial space sector, where SpaceX has long dominated.

articles.title: Spyro the Dragon returns with a new game after almost two decades
articles.summaryB1:

Spyro is a purple dragon who first appeared on the PlayStation console in the late 1990s. He quickly became a popular mascot for a whole generation of young gamers. However, the last original Spyro game came out in 2008, so fans have been waiting a long time for something new.

In this new game, Spyro has a fresh new look but still has his trademark purple colour and iconic hairstyle. The original voice actor, Tom Kenny, is returning to give Spyro his voice. One exciting feature is that players can now fly freely at any time. The creative director explained that players can dive, flap their wings, and even use fire-breath to interact with the environment. The developers want the game to inspire feelings of joy and fun. This announcement has made many nostalgic fans very happy.

Voice actor Tom Kenny, who originated the role, is reprising his performance — a detail likely to resonate strongly with long-term fans. articles.title: Trump to meet AI leaders to discuss US investment in their companies
articles.summaryB1:
US President Donald Trump has announced that he plans to meet with the leaders of some of the biggest artificial intelligence companies in the United States next week. The meetings are expected to focus on investment in these AI companies, which means the government may give or encourage large amounts of money to help them grow.

Artificial intelligence, or AI, is technology that allows computers to think and learn in ways that are similar to humans. It is used in many areas of daily life, such as search engines, healthcare, and transport. AI is one of the fastest-growing industries in the world right now.

The US government is very interested in making sure that America stays ahead in the global AI race, especially compared to countries like China. By meeting with AI leaders, Trump wants to show that his administration supports the technology sector and wants to attract more business to the country.

This kind of high-level meeting between a president and company leaders is significant because it can lead to big changes in how money is spent and how new technology is developed. articles.summaryB1: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently met with some of Europe's strongest supporters of Ukraine. Ukraine and its allies want to make sure that any peace deal does not reward Russia for its actions. The five conditions show that Ukraine is not willing to accept just any agreement. articles.title: We need to stop AI developing without humans, says Anthropic co-founder
articles.summaryB1:

Anthropic is one of the most important companies working on AI technology today. It was created by people who wanted to make sure AI develops in a safe and responsible way. Clark believes that if we are not careful, AI systems could reach a point where they improve and grow without human input. This means humans might lose control over how the technology changes.

This is a serious warning because AI is already being used in many areas of life, including medicine, business, and education. If AI starts to develop without human guidance, it could make decisions that affect people in ways that are difficult to predict or stop.

Clark's message is clear: we need to act now to make sure humans stay in control of AI development. He is calling on governments, companies, and scientists to work together to create better rules and safety systems. Many people agree that without proper oversight, the rapid growth of AI could bring serious risks to society. This story highlights why responsible AI development is so important.

This event reminds us how challenging and sometimes dangerous life in space can be, even during routine operations.

This is important because tensions between Israel and Iran have been very high recently, and many people are worried about a larger conflict starting in the region. Trump believes that a deal between Iran and Israel is the best way to bring peace and stability to the area. Netanyahu has not yet publicly agreed to follow Trump's advice, but Trump seems confident that the Israeli leader will eventually accept the agreement. This situation matters because the United States plays a very powerful role in Middle East politics, and Trump's strong language shows that he wants to be in control of how the situation develops. Many people around the world are watching closely to see what happens next.

articles.summaryB2: Donald Trump has declared that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will have 'no choice' but to accept a prospective nuclear deal with Iran, signalling a striking assertion of American dominance over its closest Middle Eastern ally. Speaking to the Financial Times, the US president insisted that he 'calls the shots' in the region, a remark widely interpreted as a pointed rebuke to Netanyahu, whom Trump had previously urged to refrain from retaliating against Tehran following recent hostilities. The statement underscores a notable shift in Washington's approach, with Trump appearing to prioritise diplomatic engagement with Iran over unconditional support for Israeli military objectives. This puts the two leaders on a potential collision course, as Netanyahu has long advocated a hardline stance towards Iran and has shown little appetite for concessions. Critics argue that Trump's blunt rhetoric risks undermining the credibility of the US-Israel alliance, while supporters contend that Washington must exert firm leverage to prevent a broader regional escalation. The situation is further complicated by Iran's ongoing nuclear programme, which Israel regards as an existential threat. By publicly pressuring Netanyahu in this manner, Trump appears to be staking out a unilateral position ahead of any formal negotiations, raising questions about how much genuine diplomatic groundwork has been laid and whether such a deal is genuinely achievable.

vocabularyB2.definition: A confident and forceful statement or claim about something

Things you agree to give up or accept in order to reach an agreement
A rapid increase in the seriousness or intensity of a conflict or problem
Done by only one country or person, without agreement from others involved

articles.questionB1: Do you think Netanyahu will accept a deal with Iran to bring stability to the region, or will tensions continue to grow?
articles.questionB2: To what extent does Trump's unilateral assertion that he 'calls the shots' risk damaging the US-Israel alliance and reducing America's credibility as a diplomatic partner?

articles.title: EU Plans Major Investment in Eastern European Transport Links
articles.summaryB1: The European Union is planning to spend a lot of money on roads and railways near its eastern borders. This will help countries like Poland, Lithuania and Romania to connect better with the rest of Europe. EU leaders agreed that better transport links are very important for the economy and for security. The money will come from a special EU fund. Work on the new roads and railways is expected to start next year. Many people who live near the border are happy about this decision. They hope that better infrastructure will also bring more jobs to their region. Poland will receive one of the largest shares of the total funding because it has a very long eastern border with Ukraine and Belarus. Local governments in Poland are already making detailed plans for how to use the money effectively.

vocabularyB1.definition: The basic systems a country needs, like roads, railways and power supplies
Money given for a specific purpose
Roads, railways and other connections that allow people to travel between places
A large area of a country with particular characteristics
In a way that works well and produces the right result

articles.summaryB2: The European Commission has unveiled a comprehensive package to bolster transport and logistical infrastructure along the EU's eastern flank, with particular emphasis on Poland, the Baltic states and Romania. The initiative draws on the Cohesion Fund and newly established defence-linked financing instruments, aiming to dual-purpose civilian infrastructure for potential military mobility requirements — a concept increasingly central to NATO's strategic posture. Poland stands to receive a disproportionately large allocation given the considerable extent of its eastern border with Ukraine and Belarus. Critics have raised legitimate questions about procurement timelines and the adequacy of environmental impact assessments, while several MEPs have called for greater transparency in the tendering process. Proponents argue that the security and economic rationale is compelling, particularly in the context of ongoing geopolitical uncertainty in the region.

articles.questionB2: Given the dual-purpose nature of this infrastructure funding, how effectively can the EU balance genuine civilian development needs against its evolving geopolitical and military mobility priorities?

articles.title: Tech Giants Face New EU Digital Rules From Autumn
articles.summaryB1: Big technology companies like Google and Meta will have to follow new rules in Europe from this autumn. The rules are part of a plan to make the internet safer and more fair for everyone. Companies that break the rules can be fined a lot of money — up to ten percent of their total income worldwide. European countries, including Poland, have strongly supported these new regulations. Users will have more control over their personal information and how large companies use it. The new rules also mean that big companies cannot use unfair methods to stop smaller companies from competing with them. Poland's digital ministry has been one of the most active supporters of strict enforcement of these rules. Many Polish internet users say they feel better protected by these changes.

vocabularyB1.definition: Official rules made by a government or authority that must be followed
The process of making sure that rules or laws are actually followed
Required to pay money as a punishment for breaking a rule or law
Trying to be more successful than others who are selling similar products or services
Kept safe from harm, danger or unfair treatment

articles.summaryB2: The Digital Markets Act enforcement timeline has been accelerated, with the European Commission confirming that designated 'gatekeepers' — including Alphabet, Meta and Apple — must demonstrate full compliance by October. The regulation targets anti-competitive behaviour, mandatory interoperability between platforms, and greater algorithmic transparency. Poland's digital ministry has been notably vocal in pushing for stricter enforcement mechanisms, reflecting broader Central European frustration with the perceived dominance of American platforms in local media ecosystems. Non-compliance carries penalties of up to 10% of global annual turnover, with repeat offenders potentially facing structural remedies including forced divestiture. Legal analysts widely expect several major platforms to challenge specific provisions in the Court of Justice of the EU.

vocabularyB2.definition: Companies that control access to important digital markets or platforms
The ability of different digital systems or applications to work together seamlessly

articles.questionB2: Given that gatekeepers may challenge key provisions in court, how realistic is it to expect full compliance and meaningful algorithmic transparency by October?

articles.title: Central European Cities Plant Thousands of Trees to Beat the Heat
articles.summaryB1: Cities in Central Europe, including Warsaw and Prague, are planting many new trees and building parks to deal with very hot summers. Scientists say that cities are getting hotter because of climate change. Green spaces help to cool the air and make life more comfortable for people living there. Local governments are spending large amounts of money on these projects. In Warsaw, the city plans to plant thousands of new trees along busy streets over the next three years. Prague is also creating several new parks in areas where there were previously only buildings and concrete. Both cities say that green areas are not just nice to look at — they are necessary for people's health during periods of extreme heat. Residents in both cities say they are happy that their local governments are taking this problem seriously.

vocabularyB1.definition: Long-term changes in global temperatures and weather patterns, mainly caused by human activities
Temperatures that are much higher than usual and can be dangerous to people's health
People who live permanently in a particular place or area
A hard building material made from cement, sand and water, used for roads and buildings
At an earlier time; before the current situation existed

articles.summaryB2: Municipal authorities across Central Europe are implementing so-called 'sponge city' strategies as urban heat islands intensify under accelerating climate projections. Warsaw's latest urban masterplan earmarks 18% of all new development land for permeable surfaces and expanding tree canopy, while Kraków has introduced mandatory heat-resilience requirements into its building regulations. Urban planners acknowledge a fundamental tension between densification pressures — driven by acute housing shortages — and the ecological imperative to preserve green corridors that regulate urban microclimates. Research from the Warsaw University of Life Sciences suggests mature street trees can reduce local temperatures by up to 8°C on peak summer days, lending considerable scientific weight to what critics had previously dismissed as a purely aesthetic concern.

vocabularyB2.definition: City areas significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to buildings, roads and human activity
Ground surfaces that allow rainwater to pass through rather than run off into drains
The process of increasing the number of buildings and population density in an urban area

articles.questionB1: How do you think planting trees and creating green spaces can help residents stay healthy during periods of extreme heat in cities?
articles.questionB2: Given the tension between densification and preserving green corridors, how should city planners balance housing shortages with the need to reduce urban heat islands?

articles.title: European Central Bank Signals Cautious Approach to Interest Rates
articles.summaryB1: The European Central Bank says it will be very careful about changing interest rates this year. Interest rates affect how much it costs to borrow money from a bank. When rates are high, people pay more for mortgages and business loans. The bank is worried about inflation, which means the prices of everyday things going up faster than usual. Poland is not part of the eurozone and uses the zloty, but decisions made by the European Central Bank still have an important effect on Poland's economy. Many Polish businesses borrow money in euros, so changes in European interest rates affect them directly. Economists say that the bank wants to be sure that inflation is really under control before it makes any big changes. This cautious approach means that borrowing will remain expensive for some time.

vocabularyB1.definition: The percentage charged by a bank for lending money, or paid on savings
A general increase in prices over time, reducing what you can buy with the same amount of money
Loans taken from a bank to buy a house or flat, repaid over many years
The group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency
Being careful and not taking risks; not acting too quickly

articles.summaryB2: The ECB's governing council has signalled a more cautious approach to further monetary easing, citing persistent services inflation and wage growth that remains above pre-pandemic trends. The hawkish tone, communicated through President Christine Lagarde's carefully worded forward guidance, has prompted a modest repricing of rate expectations in European swap markets. For Poland and other non-eurozone Central European economies, the ECB's stance indirectly constrains the National Bank of Poland's room for manoeuvre, given the zloty's well-documented sensitivity to euro-area monetary conditions. Analysts at several Warsaw-based investment banks have consequently revised their forecasts for domestic rate cuts, pushing expected reductions further into the second half of the year.

vocabularyB2.definition: Central bank policy of reducing interest rates to stimulate economic activity and borrowing

articles.questionB2: Given the ECB's hawkish forward guidance, how much room for manoeuvre does the National Bank of Poland realistically have when deciding its own rate policy?

articles.title: Polish Film Industry Gains Growing International Recognition
articles.summaryB1: Polish films are becoming more popular and well-known around the world. Three Polish films have been selected for important international film festivals this year. Film-makers from Poland say they want to tell stories about Polish history and modern Polish life in ways that people from other countries can also understand and enjoy. Streaming services like Netflix are very interested in Polish content and are spending more money on Polish productions. More young people in Poland are now choosing to study film-making at university. Industry experts say that Polish cinema has a unique voice that audiences around the world are beginning to appreciate. Warsaw is becoming an increasingly important European centre for film and television production, attracting foreign productions that use Polish studios and local talent.

vocabularyB1.definition: Events where films from different countries are shown and sometimes given prizes
Films, TV shows or other media that have been made
Online platforms like Netflix where you can watch films and shows over the internet
Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else

articles.summaryB2: Poland's cinematic output is attracting sustained international attention, with three features shortlisted for major festivals including Venice and Toronto. Analysts attribute this momentum partly to co-production frameworks with German and French broadcasters, and partly to a generational shift in domestic storytelling — younger directors are engaging with post-communist memory and contemporary Polish identity in formally adventurous and internationally accessible ways. Netflix's Warsaw-based content team has reportedly doubled its commissioning budget for Polish-language originals, signalling growing confidence that Polish narratives can translate successfully across diverse global markets. Warsaw is increasingly positioning itself as a significant Central European production hub.

articles.title: AI Tools Reshape Hiring Practices Across Europe
articles.summaryB1: Many European companies are now using artificial intelligence to help them find new employees. AI tools can look through hundreds of job applications very quickly and identify the most suitable candidates. Some people are worried that AI is not always fair when it chooses which candidates to select for interviews. In Poland, companies in the IT and finance sectors are using these tools the most. Workers are strongly advised to write their CVs in ways that AI screening systems will score positively. Trade unions across Europe are calling for new laws to protect job seekers from being unfairly rejected by automated systems. Some countries are already introducing rules that require companies to tell applicants when AI has been used in their selection process.

vocabularyB1.definition: Computer systems that can do tasks that normally require human intelligence, like making decisions

articles.summaryB2: The adoption of AI-driven applicant tracking systems has accelerated sharply across European labour markets, with a recent survey indicating that 62% of companies with over 500 employees now deploy algorithmic screening at some stage of their recruitment process. The practice raises significant compliance questions under the EU AI Act's high-risk classification for employment-related AI applications, which mandates meaningful human oversight and regular bias auditing. Polish labour lawyers note a persistent gap between the regulation's stated intent and actual enforcement capacity, particularly among mid-sized firms that lack dedicated compliance functions. Meanwhile, trade union confederations in several EU member states are lobbying for more prescriptive transparency requirements, including mandatory disclosure of AI involvement to all unsuccessful applicants.

articles.questionB2: Given the persistent gap between the EU AI Act's intent and enforcement, how effective can mandatory disclosure of algorithmic screening realistically be in protecting job seekers?

articles.title: Poland Expands Renewable Energy Capacity With New Wind Farms
articles.summaryB1: Poland is building many new wind farms to produce more clean electricity. The government wants to reduce the country's dependence on coal, which Poland has used for energy for a very long time. New wind farms are being built both on land and in the Baltic Sea. The energy from these wind farms will be enough to power millions of Polish homes. Many people support this change because it will also help to reduce air pollution in Polish cities. However, some people who live near the new wind farms are concerned about the noise and the effect on the local landscape. The Polish government says that renewable energy will create thousands of new jobs in the coming years. Poland has set a goal to produce 50% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2035.

articles.summaryB2: Poland is accelerating its offshore and onshore wind capacity in a significant pivot away from its historically coal-dependent energy mix. Several large-scale Baltic Sea wind projects have recently received government approval, with combined capacity sufficient to power an estimated four million households. The transition carries both economic and geopolitical dimensions — reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels while positioning Poland to meet its EU climate commitments under the revised Fit for 55 package. Industry analysts note that the rapid expansion will require substantial investment in grid infrastructure and storage capacity to manage intermittency. Local opposition movements, particularly in rural Mazovia and Pomerania, continue to contest planning decisions on aesthetic and ecological grounds.

articles.title: Rising Food Prices Put Pressure on European Households
articles.summaryB1: Food prices across Europe have been rising for several months, and families are finding it harder to afford their weekly shopping. In Poland, the prices of basic products like bread, milk and vegetables have gone up significantly. Economists say that bad weather affecting crops, higher transport costs and global supply problems are all contributing to the problem. Many families in Poland are changing their shopping habits — buying fewer luxury items and looking for cheaper alternatives to their usual products. Food banks in major Polish cities report that more people are coming to them for help than at any time in the past five years. The Polish government has announced some measures to help lower-income families cope with the higher prices, including an expansion of the food assistance programme.

articles.summaryB2: Persistent food price inflation is compounding cost-of-living pressures for households across the EU, with Poland among the member states experiencing above-average increases in staple food categories. A convergence of factors — including severe drought conditions affecting southern European agricultural output, elevated logistics costs, and residual supply chain disruptions — has sustained upward price pressure despite broader headline inflation easing. Polish consumer confidence indices have declined for the third consecutive quarter, with discretionary spending contracting sharply. NGOs operating food assistance networks in Warsaw and Kraków report a marked increase in first-time users, suggesting that financial distress is penetrating demographics not previously associated with food insecurity.

articles.title: European Space Agency Selects New Astronaut Class Including Eastern Europeans
articles.summaryB1: The European Space Agency has chosen a new group of astronauts, and for the first time the selection includes candidates from Central and Eastern European countries. This is seen as an important moment for the region. The new astronauts will spend years training before they can go to space. Training takes place at the ESA centre in Cologne, Germany, and also at NASA facilities in the United States. The ESA said it received more than 22,000 applications from across Europe, which is a new record. The selection of astronauts from Eastern Europe is part of a wider effort to make the space programme more representative of all EU member states. Young people across Poland and neighbouring countries have reacted with great excitement to the news.

articles.summaryB2: The European Space Agency's latest astronaut cohort marks a notable shift in the programme's geographical composition, with candidates from Central and Eastern European member states securing places for the first time in the agency's history. The selection, drawn from a record 22,500 applicants, reflects both ESA's strategic commitment to broadening institutional representation and growing political pressure from newer EU members to secure meaningful participation in flagship European scientific endeavours. The successful candidates will undergo an intensive two-year basic training curriculum at ESA's European Astronaut Centre in Cologne before becoming eligible for mission assignments. Space agency officials indicated that expanded collaboration agreements with NASA and JAXA will provide additional mission opportunities for the enlarged astronaut corps.

articles.title: Warsaw Emerges as Major European Start-Up Hub
articles.summaryB1: Warsaw is becoming one of the most important cities in Europe for new technology companies, known as start-ups. More and more young entrepreneurs from Poland and neighbouring countries are choosing Warsaw as the place to build their businesses. The city has good universities that produce talented graduates, and living costs are lower than in cities like London or Berlin. Several large international companies have recently opened technology offices in Warsaw. The Polish government has also introduced special programmes to help new businesses get started, including easier access to funding. Warsaw's growing reputation as a technology centre is attracting investors from across Europe and from the United States. Many tech workers who left Poland to work abroad are now returning to take advantage of the new opportunities available in their home city.

The opinion that people in general have about someone or something

articles.summaryB2: Warsaw is consolidating its position as one of Central Europe's premier technology ecosystems, attracting venture capital inflows and talent at a pace that is beginning to rival established Western European hubs. The city's competitive advantages — a deep pool of technically skilled graduates from Polish universities, relatively low operational costs compared to Berlin or Amsterdam, and improving quality of urban life — are proving persuasive to founders and international corporations alike. Poland's favourable regulatory environment for early-stage companies, combined with EU single market access, has made Warsaw an increasingly attractive domicile for start-ups seeking pan-European scalability. A notable reverse migration trend has seen Polish tech professionals returning from London and Zurich, bringing international networks and experience back to the domestic ecosystem.

articles.title: UNESCO Adds New Central European Sites to World Heritage List
articles.summaryB1: UNESCO, the United Nations organisation that protects important cultural and natural places around the world, has added several new Central European sites to its World Heritage List. The list includes places that are considered to have outstanding value for all of humanity. One of the new sites is in Poland, and Poles are very proud of this recognition. Being on the UNESCO list helps to attract tourists and also brings money for restoration and protection work. Local communities near the new sites are preparing for more visitors. The Polish government has promised to invest in better facilities for tourists at the site. UNESCO experts praised the site for its exceptional historical significance and its excellent state of preservation. This is Poland's fifteenth entry on the prestigious World Heritage List.

articles.summaryB2: UNESCO's World Heritage Committee has inscribed several new Central European properties on its canonical list at its annual session, with Poland's latest nomination receiving particular acclaim for the exceptional integrity of its surviving fabric and its layered historical significance spanning multiple centuries. The inscription is expected to generate a measurable uplift in cultural tourism, though heritage management specialists have cautioned that increased visitor footfall must be carefully managed to avoid the site deterioration that has affected over-touristed World Heritage properties elsewhere in Europe. Polish conservation authorities have committed to developing a comprehensive visitor management strategy in consultation with local stakeholders. The listing represents Poland's fifteenth World Heritage inscription, reinforcing the country's considerable standing in European cultural patrimony.

articles.title: EU Summit Reaches Agreement on Migration Policy Reform
articles.summaryB1: European Union leaders have reached an agreement on new rules for managing the arrival of migrants and refugees in Europe. The negotiations were very difficult and took a long time because different countries have very different opinions on this issue. Poland and other Central European countries argued strongly for stricter border controls and for sharing the responsibility for migrants more fairly among all EU members. The new agreement includes plans to process asylum applications more quickly and to increase cooperation between EU countries on returns. Some human rights organisations have criticised the agreement, saying it does not do enough to protect vulnerable people. The EU leaders say the new system will be more efficient and more fair for everyone involved. The agreement still needs to be approved by the European Parliament before it can become law.

articles.summaryB2: EU leaders have reached a qualified majority agreement on a sweeping reform of the bloc's migration and asylum architecture, ending years of institutional deadlock that had paralysed the Common European Asylum System. The compromise, which required significant concessions from both frontline Mediterranean states and Visegrad Group countries including Poland, introduces accelerated border procedures, a mandatory solidarity mechanism with financial opt-out provisions, and enhanced operational cooperation with third countries on readmission. Critics from humanitarian organisations argue that the expedited procedures risk undermining adequate due process safeguards, while Eurosceptic governments contend the solidarity mechanism still places disproportionate obligations on member states. Ratification by the European Parliament is expected to be contentious.
